papers.title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
papers.abstract: Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. EC offers an endogenous model for investigating the mechanisms of consciousness. In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Meta-analytic cognitive decoding linked EC to perceptual clarity and attentional processes, and away from distress-related domains. papers.title: Mindfulness-based interventions for sleep disturbances, physical symptoms, and biological outcomes in women with cancer: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Insomnia is prevalent among women with cancer and often co-occurs with fatigue, pain, and physiological dysregulation, yet these domains are rarely examined together in mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) research. OBJECTIVE: To map the evidence on MBIs for insomnia in this population and examined how physical symptoms and biological outcomes have been assessed alongside sleep. METHODS: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, eight databases were searched from inception to January 2026. Eligible studies included adult women with cancer receiving an MBI and reporting sleep outcomes. Data were charted on study characteristics, intervention features, sleep measures, physical symptoms, and biomarkers, and synthesized using tables and visual mapping. RESULTS: Thirty-nine studies were included. Most reported improvements in sleep, while fewer assessed fatigue, pain, or other physical symptoms, and only a small subset included biological markers. Concordance across sleep, physical, and biological domains was limited, with substantial heterogeneity in intervention format and dose. CONCLUSIONS: MBIs consistently improve sleep in women with cancer, but multidomain (sleep, physical, biological) integration remains limited due to heterogeneity. Heterogeneity in populations, interventions, comparators, and outcome measures precludes broad implementation across oncology settings. Standardized, adequately powered, mechanism-informed studies are needed to identify the most appropriate MBIs for specific patient groups and clinical contexts.

papers.title: Meditation Breathing Training and Short-Term Recovery in Patients Undergoing Thoracoscopic Lung Cancer Resection: A Non-Randomized Historical-Control Study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association of meditation breathing training with short-term physical and mental recovery in lung cancer patients after thoracoscopic lobectomy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A non-randomized historical control study design was adopted. A total of 62 patients (31 per group) diagnosed with lung cancer and receiving thoracoscopic surgery at our hospital between January 2023 and June 2024 were enrolled. Patients were allocated by admission period: 31 patients admitted from January to September 2023 were set as the control group (routine care and standard breathing training); another 31 patients admitted from October 2023 to June 2024 were assigned to the experimental group (additional meditation breathing training, twice daily for 10 minutes, from postoperative day 2 to discharge). Randomization and blinding were not applied. The primary outcome was exercise capacity (6-minute walk test, 6MWT); secondary outcomes included dyspnea (Borg scale), pain (Visual Analogue Scale, VAS), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, HADS), training compliance, and postoperative recovery indicators. RESULTS: Following the completion of the targeted intervention, the experimental group showed greater improvements in exercise capacity (adjusted mean difference: +51.64 m; 95% CI: 17.28 to 86.00), dyspnea (adjusted mean difference: -0.65; 95% CI: -1.11 to -0.19), pain (adjusted mean difference: -0.52; 95% CI: -1.00 to -0.04), and anxiety (adjusted mean difference: -1.37; 95% CI: -2.43 to -0.30), and higher training compliance (87.1% vs 64.5%; OR: 3.71; 95% CI: 1.04 to 13.25) compared with the control group; however, the between-group differences in the primary outcomes did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni correction (adjusted P = 0.019, 0.034, 0.173, 0.064, and 1.000 for exercise capacity, dyspnea, pain, anxiety, and depression, respectively). No significant between-group differences were observed for depression scores, postoperative pulmonary complications, chest tube duration, or hospital stay. CONCLUSION: In this non-randomized historical-control study, meditation breathing training was associated with improvements in selected short‑term outcomes including exercise capacity, dyspnea, and training compliance; suggestive reductions in pain and anxiety were also observed, though these did not retain statistical significance after Bonferroni correction. Confirmatory randomized controlled trials are required.

papers.title: Self-Guided Beta-Responsive Visual Neurofeedback in a Public Exhibition: Feasibility and Usability Randomized Controlled rial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurofeedback is studied for stress and anxiety regulation, but most systems require supervision or research-grade equipment. Consumer electroencephalography (EEG) could broaden access, yet autonomous first-contact feasibility, usability, and baseline neural-state effects remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: We assessed autonomous completion and usability, tested whether a fixed breathing pacer improved outcomes over visual neurofeedback alone, and explored whether pretask resting beta was associated with usability. METHODS: We conducted a single-session, 2-arm randomized feasibility and usability trial at a public science exhibition in Bern, Switzerland, between March and June 2025. Eligible adults were aged 18 years or older, could read German or French, and reported no epilepsy or implanted electronic device. A tablet app guided participants without experimenter assistance through consent, setup, a 30-second eyes-closed baseline, 1:1 randomization, a 120-second beta-responsive task, and questionnaires. The final analytic sample included participants assigned to visual neurofeedback only (VN; n=27) or visual neurofeedback plus a 6 breaths/minute breathing pacer (VN+BP; n=25). Outcomes were usability, relaxation, and state mindfulness. Data were collected prospectively; no secondary data were used. Analyses used Mann-Whitney  RESULTS: Of 110 visitors initiating a session, 79 completed the task with a valid EEG recording (71.8%, 95% CI 62.8-79.4) and 52 met analytic criteria (47.3%, 95% CI 38.2%-56.5%). Participants (35 women) had a mean age of 39.0 (SD 11.3) years. Usability was good (System Usability Scale [SUS] mean 72.3, SD 14.7; 95% CI 68.3-76.2), and 31/52 participants scored at least 68 (59.6%, 95% CI 46.1%-71.8%). Usability did not differ between VN and VN+BP (median 75.0, IQR 62.5-81.3 vs median 72.5, IQR 65.0-90.0; Mann-Whitney  CONCLUSIONS: This trial evaluated an autonomous consumer-EEG neurofeedback system integrating self-fitting, signal-quality checking, baseline calibration, adaptive feedback, randomization, and self-report without operator support. Many first-time users completed the autonomous workflow with acceptable-to-good usability; a fixed, open-loop breathing pacer did not improve usability, relaxation, or state mindfulness; and higher resting beta showed a preliminary association with lower perceived usability. These findings support autonomous consumer-EEG neurofeedback and motivate work on adaptive onboarding, validated EEG pipelines, and objective self-regulation outcomes.

papers.title: Non Pharmacological Pain Management in Sickle Cell Disease, a Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pain is a major cause of morbidity, disability, and reduced quality of life among people living with sickle cell disease (SCD). Although pharmacological treatment remains essential, non pharmacological interventions may provide complementary strategies for pain coping and symptom management. However, the strength of evidence supporting individual interventions varies considerably. OBJECTIVE: This narrative review aimed to critically evaluate the evidence for non pharmacological interventions used to manage acute and chronic pain in SCD, distinguish disease-specific findings from indirect evidence, identify limitations in the literature, and discuss implications for clinical practice and resource-constrained settings. METHODS: The review examined randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, observational studies, systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines addressing non pharmacological pain management in SCD. The evidence covered psychological and behavioral interventions, physical and sensory approaches, technology-assisted interventions, and supportive coping practices. Original SCD-specific studies were prioritized when evaluating intervention effectiveness. Findings from other chronic pain populations were treated as contextual evidence rather than proof of effectiveness in SCD. RESULTS: The evidence was most developed for selected psychological and behavioral interventions, particularly cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and biofeedback in pediatric populations. In a multicenter randomized controlled trial involving adolescents with SCD, a digital CBT intervention was associated with a greater reduction in average pain intensity and fewer pain days at six months than an education control. Pediatric systematic reviews also identified studies investigating massage, virtual reality, yoga, and biofeedback; however, the evidence was limited by intervention heterogeneity, small sample sizes, methodological limitations, and inconsistent outcome reporting. The American Society of Hematology conditionally recommended massage, yoga, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), virtual reality, and guided audiovisual relaxation as adjuncts for acute SCD pain, based on very-low-certainty evidence. The available evidence for TENS was insufficient to establish benefit or harm. SCD-specific evidence for acupuncture, mindfulness-based interventions, hypnosis, and spiritual interventions was insufficient to establish their comparative analgesic effectiveness. CONCLUSION: Non pharmacological interventions may complement pharmacological treatment and support pain coping in SCD, but their effectiveness should be evaluated individually rather than assumed across intervention categories. Clinical decisions should consider patient preferences, intervention-specific evidence, clinical circumstances, safety, and local resources. Larger controlled trials and implementation studies, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and other low- and middle-income countries, are needed.

papers.title: Lifestyle Psychiatry in Mental Health Care: Knowledge, Practices and Attitudes of Australian Health Practitioners.
papers.abstract: This study sought to examine Australian health practitioners' knowledge, practices, and attitudes regarding lifestyle psychiatry to help elucidate factors driving an implementation gap. A convergent parallel mixed methods design was employed using an online survey with closed- and open-ended questions on eight lifestyle interventions. 212 eligible health practitioners working in or referring to mental health settings completed an online survey. Descriptive analyses were used for quantitative data, and conventional content analysis for qualitative data. Results indicated that 73.6% of participants had knowledge of lifestyle psychiatry. Two categories described their understanding of lifestyle psychiatry in mental health care: Lifestyle interventions are non-medical adjuncts that complement current practices; and lifestyle interventions empower behaviour change across a range of domains. Most participants considered all eight lifestyle interventions to be evidence-based. The mean number of lifestyle interventions in which participants had received additional training was 1.65, most commonly in mindfulness and stress reduction. Five categories were constructed from respondents' perceived benefits of lifestyle interventions: psychological health, physical health, self-empowerment, holistic wellbeing, and connection to self, other and the wider context. Perceived risks fell into three categories: psychological distress, physical harm, and social and economic impacts. Incorporation of lifestyle psychiatry into patient care varied across interventions; dietary interventions and smoking cessation had the largest implementation gap. Overall, respondents identified benefits of lifestyle psychiatry for holistic mental health care but limited integration, possibly due to perceived risks and insufficient training. Findings support calls for strengthened professional development and embedded training in lifestyle psychiatry within health degrees.

papers.title: Beyond adversity: Dispositional mindfulness as a potential link between positive childhood experiences and lower hair cortisol concentration in adulthood.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Advers childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with altered stress regulation, yet less is known about how positive childhood experiences (PCEs) contribute to adaptive physiological functioning. PCEs may represent developmental resources that promote adaptive psychological and biological functioning. This study examined whether PCEs were associated with cumulative cortisol exposure, indexed by hair cortisol concentration (HCC), through dispositional mindfulness and resilience, and whether these associations varied according to cumulative childhood adversity. METHODS: A community sample of 210 adults (M age = 28.95, SD = 10.20, range = 19-77; 74.8% female) completed an online assessment battery. A subsample of 120 participants provided hair samples for cortisol assessment. Participants completed measures of Protective and Compensatory experiences (PACE significance), ACEs, dispositional mindfulness (MAAS), resilience (RS-14), and current stress (LSC-R). Hair cortisol concentration (HCC) from 3 cm proximal segment was assessed as an indicator of cumulative hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity. RESULTS: PACE sig. showed indirect association with lower HCC through greater dispositional mindfulness, whereas resilience did not. Moderation analyses suggested that the positive PACE sig.-MAAS association was stronger at higher levels of ACE exposure. Positive and adverse childhood experiences frequently co-occurred among participants with higher cumulative adversity. CONCLUSIONS: These findings extend existing evidence on the psychological benefits associated with PCEs by providing preliminary support for dispositional mindfulness as a potential link between PCEs and lower cumulative cortisol exposure in adulthood. Considering positive developmental experiences alongside adversity may improve understanding of individual differences in psychological functioning and long-term HPA-axis activity.
